claims.text: Enhanced free-energy sampling integrated with molecular dynamics will more accurately quantify the size-dependent thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
The improved quantification will result from capturing rare thermal events.
The initial material consists of synthesized FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with controlled size distributions.
Molecular dynamics can be used to investigate the atomic-scale thermal behavior of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Heating high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can produce surface-layer melting, phase separation, and pronounced atomic diffusion.
FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles of different sizes should be compared under identical thermodynamic conditions.
Free-energy barriers governing melting and phase transitions depend on FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticle size.
Nanoparticle size alters diffusion pathways that govern melting and phase-transition phenomena.
Enhanced sampling methods efficiently overcome energy barriers during molecular dynamics simulations.
Enhanced sampling captures melting or phase-separation events that are obscured in conventional molecular dynamics.
Enhanced sampling permits determination of how the free-energy landscape changes with nanoparticle size.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will have lower free-energy barriers for melting or phase transformation than larger nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will have lower melting or phase-transformation temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
Conventional molecular dynamics may miss rare thermal events and produce incomplete or misleading thermal-stability profiles.
The hypothesis is limited to the simulated temperature range, nanoparticle sizes, and simulation time window.
Precise free-energy differences and transition temperatures require calibration against experimental data.
Multi-element interactions introduce uncertainty into computed energy barriers.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing conventional and enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics across multiple nanoparticle sizes.
A lack of correlation between nanoparticle size and measured transition parameters would falsify the predicted size dependence.
